strengths: The paper investigates an important and timely question—how Diffusion Transformers internally implement compositional spatial-relational generation—using a mechanistic interpretability framework (attention synopsis, head ablation, causal VO injection, variance partitioning). This is a meaningful and underexplored direction.

The experimental design is rigorous and well controlled: a synthetic dataset with clean ground-truth relations, a deterministic OpenCV-based evaluator, multiple model scales (nano/mini/micro/B), and two distinct text-encoder regimes (RTE with and without positional encoding, and pretrained T5). This allows clean causal attribution.

The discovered RTE-DiT circuit is non-trivial and convincingly supported: a two-stage mechanism in which a 'spatial relation head' (L2H8) converts relational text into positional-gradient tags via a QK circuit, and an 'object generation head' (L4H3) reads those tags to bind shape tokens to locations. Evidence includes attention synopses, per-head ablation (relational accuracy 67%→33% for L2H8; 90%→76% for L4H3), consistency across model sizes, and VO-injection causally inducing the expected attention pattern.

The T5 finding that relation information is fused into a single shape2 token—validated by token-masking (relation words have little effect, shape2/EOS ablation is catastrophic) and by vector-arithmetic manipulations that shift generated relations—provides strong and surprising causal evidence.

The downstream insight that the text encoder, not the DiT, can be the bottleneck for relational generation, and the demonstrated robustness gap (RTE robust to filler words, T5 collapsing under a small lexical perturbation such as adding 'the'), is practical and would be useful for future T2I design.

Presentation is generally clear; the schematics (Figs. 4, 5, 7) effectively communicate the mechanisms, and the appendix provides extensive detail on dataset construction, training, evaluation, and statistical methodology (variance partitioning with permutation tests).
weaknesses: All models are trained from scratch on a very small, synthetic, stylized dataset (gray background, two shapes, two colors, 8 relations, 128×128). It is not shown that the identified circuits or the encoder-bottleneck conclusion transfer to large, pretrained real-world T2I systems (e.g., SD3, Flux, PixArt on natural data). The paper's framing about 'real-world scenarios' is therefore only indirectly supported.

The smallest model (DiT-nano) fails to learn spatial relations at all (5%), so the claim that the circuit mechanism 'generalizes across model sizes' has an explicit lower bound. The set of scales tested is also narrow.

The 'specialized head' identification relies on attention-synopsis aggregation heuristics, which can be sensitive to thresholds, prompt subsets, and aggregation choices; while head ablation/ VO injection provide causal support, a more thorough statistical characterization of head-specificity (e.g., across many seeds/models, confidence intervals on the dominance of L2H8/L4H3) would strengthen the claims.

Some causal claims are inferred from small effect sizes (e.g., L4H3 object-shape ablation 90%→76%) and the analysis is largely qualitative on attention maps; a stronger quantitative decomposition (e.g., path patching / activation patching) would make the circuit claim more airtight.

The variance-partitioning analysis attributes only ~12% marginal variance to spatial relation in the raw T5 embedding, which is modest; its role as evidence for the fusion claim could be strengthened by linking individual factor vectors more directly to downstream behavioral changes.

The recommendation that 'embedding-model improvements are potentially more critical than DiT modifications' is a strong conclusion drawn from a controlled toy setup and is not evaluated against any real model retrofit or finetuning experiment, so it remains speculative.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and novel mechanistic explanation of how Diffusion Transformers generate spatial relations, distinguishing between two fundamentally different circuits depending on the text encoder used (RTE vs. T5). This circuit-level understanding is a significant contribution to interpretability in generative vision models.

The use of causal interventions (ablation and manipulation) goes beyond correlational analysis, providing strong evidence for the identified roles of specific attention heads (L2H8 and L4H3). This experimental design is rigorous and well-executed.

The Attention Synopsis method is a scalable and effective technique for analyzing cross-attention patterns in diffusion transformers, enabling the discovery of specialized heads across various model sizes and prompting conditions.

The controlled synthetic dataset and exhaustive evaluation metrics allow for precise and reproducible analysis of model behavior, which is a valuable methodological contribution for studying compositional generation.

The findings have important implications for future text-to-image model design, suggesting that embedding model improvements may be more critical than architectural modifications for spatial reasoning, and that T5 embeddings fuse relational information in a more entangled but robust way compared to random embeddings.
The paper is well-organized and clearly written, with extensive supplementary material that supports the main claims and provides additional evidence for generality across model scales.

The work addresses a timely and important problem in text-to-image generation, and its mechanistic approach offers a fresh perspective compared to prior black-box evaluations or purely performance-oriented remedies.
The release of code and data upon acceptance enhances reproducibility and will facilitate further research in this direction.
weaknesses: The study is limited to a synthetic dataset with simple shapes and colors, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world spatial relations and object compositions. Generalization to natural images remains to be demonstrated.

The models trained are relatively small (up to DiT-B with 12 layers) and trained from scratch on a narrow task, so the circuits discovered might differ from those in large-scale, pretrained T2I models like Stable Diffusion or DALL-E.

The paper does not propose a direct method to improve spatial relation generation in existing models, although it provides insights that could inform such improvements. This limits the immediate practical impact.

The robustness of T5-DiT to relation word ablation but sensitivity to minor prompt perturbations (e.g., adding 'the') is an interesting finding but is not fully explained mechanistically, leaving room for further investigation.
The current analysis focuses on cross-attention; other components such as self-attention or MLP layers could also play important roles in relation generation, which are not explored in depth.

The evaluation metrics rely on a rule-based parsing system using OpenCV, which might have limitations in handling more complex or ambiguous generated images, though it is adequate for the controlled dataset.
The paper does not compare against state-of-the-art T2I models on the same synthetic task, which would help contextualize the findings and the performance of the trained DiTs.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: how diffusion transformers mechanistically compose spatial relations, and it provides a controlled comparison between pretrained T5 text embeddings and random token embeddings.

The 'attention synopsis' pipeline is a reasonable method for summarizing large numbers of cross-attention maps and identifying candidate layer-head circuits; it goes beyond purely qualitative attention visualization.

The paper supports its main RTE-DiT finding with both ablations and causal manipulation, identifying a spatial-relation head (L2H8) and an object-generation head (L4H3) and showing that perturbing these heads changes relational and object accuracy.

The T5/random-embedding comparison exposes a useful trade-off: RTE-DiT relies on a modular two-stage circuit and is robust to filler tokens but sensitive to relation-word ablation, while T5-DiT absorbs relation information into contextual token embeddings and is more sensitive to small lexical perturbations despite strong in-domain accuracy.
The manuscript is generally clear, and the appendix provides detailed dataset construction, training setup, and evaluation definitions.
weaknesses: The evidence is restricted to a highly simplified synthetic setting: 10k generated images, two distinct shapes/colors, eight spatial relations, a gray background, 128×128 resolution, and templated captions. This is far from real-world text-to-image generation and cannot by itself substantiate broad claims about spatial relation failures in modern diffusion transformers.

All models are trained from scratch and are relatively small (DiT-B/mini/micro/nano). The paper does not test large pretrained DiT systems such as PixArt-α, SD3, or FLUX, nor does it use standard compositional benchmarks like T2I-CompBench++. The central circuit findings may therefore not transfer to practical T2I models.

The circuit identification is largely correlational, with only limited causal validation. Head ablation shows L2H8 and L4H3 are important, but not that they constitute a sufficient or complete 'minimal circuit'; the VO-injection experiment demonstrates relational tagging, not full object generation. Other heads, MLP layers, and residual pathways may also contribute.

The evaluation pipeline is brittle and non-standard: it relies on OpenCV color thresholding, contour classification, and a loose spatial-relation criterion with manually chosen pixel thresholds. This may produce noisy metrics that are not directly comparable to prior work, especially in occluded or overlapping scenes.

The T5-DiT analysis overinterprets the role of the second shape token. Masking shape2 likely disrupts object identity and sentence context, not only the spatial relation, making the conclusion that relation information is uniquely encoded in shape2 difficult to isolate. The vector arithmetic result is suggestive but does not fully establish that relational geometry is linearly and causally stored in that token alone.

The paper does not demonstrate that its interpretability findings improve real spatial-relation generation in practical T2I models. The discussion that text-embedding design may be a bottleneck is plausible but remains speculative, without interventions on real large-scale systems or standard benchmarks.

Reproducibility is limited: code, configurations, and dataset will only be released upon acceptance, and some training/evaluation choices are not accompanied by error bars or multi-seed statistics across all central claims.

strengths: The paper applies mechanistic interpretability to a well-motivated and timely problem (spatial relation failure in T2I diffusion transformers) and delivers concrete, falsifiable claims about the underlying computation.

The controlled synthetic dataset (2 objects, 3 shapes, 2 colors, 8 relations) plus training DiTs from scratch is an appropriate methodology for circuit analysis, enabling clean ablations and causal manipulations that would be impossible on a black-box real model.

Identification of specific heads with causal evidence is convincing: L2H8 in RTE-DiT is shown via QK analysis, attention maps, and single-head ablation to reduce relation accuracy from 67% to 33%; L4H3 similarly affects object shape accuracy (90%→76%). The two-stage circuit hypothesis (relation head writes position tags; object head reads them) is supported by the injection experiment.

The 'Attention Synopses' method (aggregating attention into interpretable category-to-category transmission patterns, then reducing to a layer×head summary) is a practical and reusable tool for scalability over >10M attention maps.

The weight-space head screening procedure (ramp template alignment over QK inner products using positional embeddings and text features) is a novel, efficient, and testable way to localize relation heads without sampling images.

The contrast between RTE-DiT and T5-DiT circuits, and the different robustness profile to prompt perturbations (fillers, reordering, color synonyms), is an interesting and important finding with concrete supporting analyses (Fig. 27, Table 1).

Extension of the analysis to CLIP-DiT and pre-trained PixArt-Sigma demonstrates generality of the framework and shows it can surface interpretable structure even in a model with weak spatial reasoning.

Variance partitioning of the T5 contextual embedding (Table 1) and the causal vector-arithmetic manipulation (Fig. 7C) provide quantitative and causal evidence that relational geometry is encoded in the shape2 token.
Detailed and reproducible method description: dataset generation pseudocode, training hyperparameters, sampling, VAE/encoder choices, and full ablation pipelines are provided.
weaknesses: The findings are established almost entirely on a minimalist 128×128 synthetic dataset (2 shapes, 2 fixed colors, gray background). It is unclear how well the identified circuits and the RTE-vs-T5 trade-off generalize to realistic scenes, textures, and many objects, which is repeatedly foregrounded as the motivating problem.

The pre-trained model validation (PixArt-Sigma) is weak: only 8 of 30 object pairs show non-trivial relation accuracy, so the main-circuit claims cannot be strongly verified in a model with realistic spatial failure. The paper acknowledges the U-Net architecture as a limitation, but this also limits the strength of the 'transferability' claim.

Some of the headline claims are scale-dependent. The smallest RTE-DiT (nano) exhibits no relation head and ~5% relation accuracy, suggesting the circuit is a property of sufficient capacity rather than a general property of DiTs; this is acknowledged but somewhat undercuts the generality of the title's framing.

The T5-DiT 'circuit' is described as an absence of a clean relation head and a diffuse reliance on shape2/shape1 embeddings. This is a useful negative result, but the resulting 'circuit' is less well-characterized and is partly an expected consequence of T5's contextualization rather than a novel mechanistic finding.

Causal evidence for the RTE relation head is primarily from ablating one head (L2H8), which reduces (not eliminates) relation accuracy to 33% — the residual likely reflects other distributed components. The paper does not fully characterize the remaining circuit or its dependence on the injected VO signal.

The relation head's behavior is explained using QK interaction with a pretrained/sinusoidal positional embedding; the interpretation of the resulting 'spatial gradients' as a positional-tag mechanism relies on strong assumptions (e.g., that positional embeddings dominate the query) that are only partially validated.

The synthetic task uses fixed association of 'object1' with the first-named object, which makes the learning problem somewhat simplified (ordering is deterministic); real prompts often have more ambiguous referential structure.

The claim that 'T5's self-attention spreads the complete sentence context … so DiT only needs to decode relevant information from shape2' is supported by masking experiments but is not fully disentangled from the possibility that the DiT-MLP simply compresses information into the most attended token.

strengths: Original mechanistic interpretability study of spatial relation generation in diffusion transformers, going beyond black-box evaluation to identify specific attention heads and circuits.

Controlled synthetic dataset and training from scratch enable clean disentanglement of text encoder effects, model size, and architecture, with extensive quantitative analysis (attention synopsis, weight-space head screening, variance partitioning, causal ablation).

Identifies meaningful circuit differences: RTE-DiT uses a two-stage circuit with specialized relation and object generation heads (e.g., L2H8 and L4H3), while T5-DiT relies on relation information fused into the shape2 token; the analysis also transfers to CLIP-DiT and partially to PixArt-Sigma.
Causal manipulations (head ablation, vector arithmetic) and robustness experiments strengthen the claim that the discovered heads/circuits are functionally relevant rather than merely correlated.
Code and data are released, and the paper is generally clear and reproducible, with detailed appendix descriptions of dataset construction, model training, and evaluation metrics.
weaknesses: The core training/evaluation setting is a simplified synthetic dataset of two objects, three shapes, two colors, and eight spatial relations at 128x128 resolution; external validity to complex natural images and large-scale text-to-image generation is therefore limited.

Pretrained model validation is relatively narrow: PixArt-Sigma shows low spatial-relation accuracy and is analyzed on only a small set of object pairs; broader state-of-the-art diffusion transformers are not fully dissected, so generality remains partly unproven.

Evaluation relies on OpenCV-based parsing and color/contour heuristics, which may misclassify objects or relations in ambiguous cases, especially under occlusion, unusual layouts, or when generated colors/shapes deviate from the synthetic training distribution.

Robustness claims, such as the impact of inserting 'the' into prompts, are demonstrated mainly for T5-based models and would benefit from more diverse prompt perturbations and validation on real pretrained T5/CLIP encoders at scale.

The interpretability conclusions are drawn primarily from small models trained from scratch; it is not fully established how these circuit mechanisms scale to billion-parameter diffusion transformers or whether the same interventions would remain effective.

strengths: The paper performs a controlled study by training DiT models from scratch on a synthetic two-object spatial-relation dataset and comparing three conditioning regimes (RTE, T5, CLIP), which helps isolate text-encoder effects from other confounds.

It introduces and combines multiple mechanistic tools—Attention Synopsis, weight-space head screening, variance partitioning, and ablation/causal manipulation—and uses them to identify concrete components in RTE-DiT, notably a spatial relation head (L2H8) and an object generation head (L4H3).

The finding that T5-DiT differs from RTE-DiT is supported by token masking, contextual-embedding analysis, and vector arithmetic, suggesting that T5 absorbs relational information into the second object token rather than relying on direct relation-word attention.

The robustness comparison—RTE-DiT remaining relatively stable under filler-word perturbations while T5-DiT degrades—is a useful mechanistic observation, and the extension to PixArt-Sigma and CLIP-DiT suggests the analysis pipeline has some generality.

The paper tackles an important question for text-to-image generation, namely how spatial relations are encoded and implemented inside diffusion transformers, and it offers a plausible circuit-level account rather than only reporting end-task accuracy.
weaknesses: The central claims about real-world T2I behavior are built almost entirely on a synthetic toy dataset (simple shapes, two colors, gray background, 128×128 images, fixed prompt templates) and small from-scratch DiTs; there is no natural-image benchmark or convincing demonstration that the conclusions transfer to practical large-scale generation.

The mechanistic circuit findings are largely correlational and selectively causal: attention synopses and weight-space screening identify heads, but only a handful of heads are ablated, no comprehensive necessity/sufficiency analysis is given, and the T5-DiT circuit is localized mainly through inference-time token masking and vector arithmetic rather than training-time circuit interventions.

Reproducibility and experimental reporting are incomplete: the code/dataset URL in Appendix C is blank, the main T5-DiT uses an unclear weight-decay setting relative to the collapsed “T5 DiT-B WD” baseline, final metrics lack seed variance/error bars, and training compute/details are not fully reported.

The conclusions overreach the evidence: the claim that embedding-model improvements may be “more critical” than DiT modifications is not tested by actually improving an encoder or showing a real-world spatial-relation gain, and the robustness results on tiny paraphrases do not establish brittleness in realistic T2I scenarios.

Presentation is dense and appendix-dependent; key definitions and supporting analyses for variance partitioning, weight-space screening, and effect vectors are hard to assess from the main text, and some abstract claims are broader than what the main experiments substantiate.

The paper does not compare against existing interpretability or attention-guidance methods for spatial relations beyond a limited PixArt-Sigma case study, making it difficult to judge whether the proposed circuit descriptions offer unique explanatory value over prior work.
